claims.text: The initial Hf-Mo-Ta-Ti-Zr alloy is single-phase BCC.
Asymmetric XRD peaks in the initial alloy indicate compositional micro-segregation between dendritic and interdendritic regions.
The initial alloy has significantly reduced room-temperature fracture strain.
Approximately 4 at.% Cr will be added to the Hf-Mo-Ta-Ti-Zr alloy.
Adding approximately 4 at.% Cr induces precipitation of a Cr-rich, complex multicomponent Laves phase.
The Cr-induced Laves phase has a volume fraction of approximately 4%.
The Laves phase is likely a C14 or C15 structure.
The Laves phase forms at grain boundaries and in interdendritic regions.
The Laves phase develops a reticulated or interconnected network morphology.
The reticulated Laves phase impedes crack propagation through crack deflection and bridging.
Crack deflection and bridging increase fracture-surface area and energy dissipation.
Substitution involving smaller Cr atoms and larger Hf or Zr atoms contracts the BCC lattice and shifts its XRD peaks to higher 2θ.
Cr-induced lattice contraction increases lattice-distortion energy and provides solid-solution hardening.
The Cr-modified alloy will have higher room-temperature yield strength than the unmodified alloy.
The Cr-modified alloy will recover room-temperature fracture strain relative to the unmodified alloy despite containing a brittle Laves phase.
Annealing at 1000–1200 °C is sufficient for phase separation while remaining below the Laves-phase solvus and preserving the micro-segregated dendritic morphology.
In the baseline alloy, cracks propagate through the segregated BCC matrix without substantial crack deflection.
A Laves-phase fraction above approximately 10–15% would produce a continuous brittle network or catastrophic embrittlement.
The cited Laves-phase evidence concerns a Cr-Mo-Nb-W-V alloy rather than the Hf-Mo-Ta-Ti-Zr-Cr target system.
The assumption that approximately 4 vol.% Laves phase will be reticulated rather than continuous is an extrapolation not directly observed in the cited evidence.
